beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/Mongo connection string exclusively from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never commit the URI or write it to logs, files, or test fixtures.

Use a single, process-wide PyMongo MongoClient (singleton) and reuse it for all operations instead of creating a client per operation or per request; configure maxPoolSize to match expected concurrent load.
Require TLS for connections (use the connection string with tls=true/ssl=true and verify certificates); do not disable certificate verification in production.
Do not store secrets in source control; provide a .env.example with placeholders and load real secrets from environment or a secure secret store (Key Vault) at runtime.
Create an index on patientId (and on patientId plus any timestamp field used for sorting) before loading production data; make the index creation idempotent and part of seeding/migrations.
For queries that return structured summaries by patient, use a compound index keyed by (patientId, summaryType or createdAt) to support the common lookup patterns instead of collection scans.
Keep individual documents well under the 16 MB BSON document size limit (split large transcripts into separate documents or chunked segments and reference them) and enforce this in the app.

Model structured clinical summary as a small, typed document (fields: patientId, chief_complaint, assessment, plan, follow_up, createdAt, sourceTranscriptId, embeddings?) and store it in its own collection rather than embedding large transcripts.

If storing LLM embeddings for vector search, store numeric arrays in a dedicated embeddings field and create the appropriate vector index with explicit dimension and metric parameters (e.g., HNSW/IVF settings) at collection/index creation time.

When creating vector indexes, specify index metadata (dimension, distance metric like cosine or euclidean, and index type) and validate embeddings length at write time to avoid mismatched-dimension index errors.

Enable application-level retries with exponential backoff for transient network errors and MongoDB transient error codes; also enable retryableWrites=true in the connection string if supported by the server version.

Use appropriate writeConcern for the use case: for clinical summaries prefer acknowledged writes (w=majority or w=1 with journaling) rather than unacknowledged, and allow the app to surface write failures to operators.
Limit the fields returned by queries (projection) to only those needed by the caller (e.g., exclude raw transcript text when returning summary lists) to reduce bandwidth and memory usage.

Add schema validation (JSON Schema) on the summaries collection to enforce required fields and datatypes (patientId as string/UUID, createdAt as date, summary fields as strings) to catch bad writes early.
Avoid expensive unindexed queries in user-facing code; for debugging, capture and inspect query plans (explain) and watch for COLLSCANs; make index changes part of deployable migration scripts.
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral/transient data (e.g., session logs, temporary LLM caches) rather than ad-hoc deletion scripts; define the TTL field and index in the seeding/migration step.
Instrument DB calls for latency, errors and throughput and wire those metrics to Azure Monitor/Prometheus; enable server-side diagnostics/auditing for security-sensitive operations.

Treat patient-identifying data as sensitive: enable encryption at rest (platform-managed or customer-managed keys), restrict network access to the cluster (VNet/firewall) and use role-based access control for operational users.
Make seed scripts idempotent: create collections and indexes only if they do not already exist, and upsert sample patient and transcript documents to avoid duplicates in repeated runs.

In unit and smoke tests, avoid depending on production secrets or live customer data; run tests against a dedicated test database (sample_healthcare_14 in this case) and clean up test artifacts or use ephemeral namespaces.
